passage:
At the birthday party in the society hall, Yamini slipped out with her book and settled into the quiet corner behind the sofa. Music thumped, balloons burst. She turned a page, feet tucked up, smiling at nothing.
Her mother Vidya found her and crouched. "Everyone's playing musical chairs, beta. Don't you want to?"
"Not now," said Yamini. "I'm at the best part."
Vidya looked at her calm face, then at the noisy room. "Shall I bring you a plate?"
"Yes, please."
When the game ended, Yamini strolled over on her own, cheeks pink, and asked what the next round was.

qa.q: Where did Yamini settle with her book?
qa.a: In the quiet corner behind the sofa.

qa.q: How does Yamini feel in the corner, and how can you tell?
qa.a: She feels content. She smiles at nothing, tucks her feet up and says she is at the best part.

qa.q: What choice by Vidya helped Yamini's afternoon?
qa.a: Vidya looked at Yamini's calm face, did not force her to join and offered to bring a plate instead.

qa.q: What might Vidya have been thinking as she looked at the noisy room?
qa.a: She may have wondered whether Yamini was missing out, but seeing her calm face she accepted that Yamini was happy.

grounding: A child happily reads alone in a corner and feels content; forced socialising would be an intrusion.

passage:
Kashish: Cousin Karthik! Everyone's on the terrace. Why are you under the stairs?
Karthik: I'm drawing.
Kashish: You can draw on the terrace.
Karthik: It's noisy. Here it's just me and the pencil.
Kashish: Are you sad?
Karthik: No! I'm happy. I just like it here.
Kashish: Even at Diwali?
Karthik: I'll do sparklers later. Now I'm drawing a lion.
Kashish: Can I see?
Karthik: When it has a mane.
Kashish: Okay. I'll bring you a laddoo, and you tell me when it's sparkler time.
Karthik: Deal. Thanks, cousin.

qa.q: What is Karthik drawing under the stairs?
qa.a: A lion.

qa.q: What is Karthik feeling under the stairs, and how does Karthik answer the question about sadness?
qa.a: Karthik feels happy and content. Karthik says, 'No! I'm happy. I just like it here.'

qa.q: What could Kashish do to respect Karthik's choice and still stay connected?
qa.a: Kashish already brings a laddoo and lets Karthik say when it is sparkler time, so Karthik is not pushed.

qa.q: What might Kashish be thinking when asking 'Are you sad?'
qa.a: Kashish worries a little that being alone at a festival might mean sadness, and relaxes when Karthik says the alone time is a happy choice.

grounding: A child happily draws alone and feels content, and a cousin learns that wanting solitude is not sadness.

passage:
"Vijay, come out, everyone's playing antakshari!"
"In a bit, Ammi." Vijay didn't look up from the comic. He was curled in the window seat, one sock off.
Sabina came closer. "Are you sad? Did someone say something?"
"No. I'm happy. This is the best part."
"Your cousins will think you're rude."
"They're singing. They don't need me." He turned a page and grinned at a picture.
Sabina watched him for a moment. His face was relaxed, his foot swinging.
"All right," she said. "Come when you want. There's cake at eight."
"Save me the corner piece," Vijay said, already back in the story.

qa.q: What was the family playing?
qa.a: Antakshari.

qa.q: How was Vijay feeling in the window seat?
qa.a: Vijay felt happy and content, enjoying the best part of his comic on his own.

qa.q: What did Sabina do that respected Vijay's choice?
qa.a: She checked he wasn't sad, noticed his relaxed face, and let him join when he wanted, with cake at eight.

qa.q: Why might Sabina have worried at first?
qa.a: Sabina may have feared that being alone meant Vijay was sad, or that the cousins would think him rude.

grounding: Shows a child happily reading alone and content, and a parent seeing that wanting solitude is not sadness.

passage:
When I was nine, my favourite place was under the big table in our dining room. I'd take my crayons and a pile of old calendars and draw on the backs for hours. I drew whole cities, with roads and a hospital and a sweet shop.
One Saturday my friend Payal came to call me out to play. I said, "Not today." She looked surprised, then went home. I wasn't cross with her. I was just happy where I was.
My Nani worried I was lonely. I wasn't. It felt like having a room inside my head that was all mine. I'm Reena, and I still draw cities when I need quiet.

qa.q: What did Reena draw on the back of old calendars?
qa.a: Whole cities, with roads, a hospital and a sweet shop.

qa.q: How did Reena feel under the table?
qa.a: Reena felt happy and peaceful, like having a room inside the head that was all Reena's own.

qa.q: What could Nani do if she's worried Reena is lonely?
qa.a: Nani could gently ask how Reena feels, and if Reena is content, simply let the quiet time be.

qa.q: How might Payal have felt when Reena said "Not today"?
qa.a: Payal was surprised and might have felt a little turned away, though Reena wasn't cross.

grounding: Shows a child content in solitude, drawing alone for hours, which an adult misreads as loneliness.

passage:
Class 4 teacher's note, Monday.
Salma has spent every recess this week on the bench under the gulmohar tree, reading. Last week I pushed her to join the skipping group. She joined, stood at the end of the rope looking lost, and came back to the bench as soon as she could.
Today I sat with her and asked if she was okay. She smiled and said, "I like it here. The book is about a girl who lives in a lighthouse." She speaks up in class, plays with Rehaan after school and seems cheerful.
I think this is simply how she recharges. I won't push the skipping again.
Abhinav

qa.q: What is Salma's book about?
qa.a: A girl who lives in a lighthouse.

qa.q: How does Salma feel about spending recess alone?
qa.a: Salma feels content and happy, smiling and saying she likes it there.

qa.q: What did Abhinav decide, and why?
qa.a: Not to push her into skipping again, after seeing she is cheerful and connected elsewhere and simply recharges alone.

qa.q: What was being pushed into the skipping group like for Salma?
qa.a: It was uncomfortable; she stood at the end of the rope looking lost and went back to the bench as soon as she could.

grounding: Shows a child who enjoys her own company at recess, and forced socialising feeling like an intrusion.

passage:
Sunday
Today cousin Kiran came over and wanted me to play hide and seek with all the neighbourhood kids. I said I was reading. Kiran said, "You're so boring! Are you sad or something?"
I'm NOT sad. I was reading my detective book in my corner behind the almirah, with a pillow and a guava. It was the best part, where the dog finds the key.
Mummy made me go out anyway. I played for ten minutes and kept thinking about the key. It felt like someone had grabbed my book out of my hands.
When they went home, I went back to my corner. The key was in the well! I knew it!
I like being alone sometimes. It's not a sad thing. It's a quiet thing.
Aditi

qa.q: Where does Aditi read?
qa.a: Aditi reads in a corner behind the almirah, with a pillow and a guava.

qa.q: How did Aditi feel when made to go out and play?
qa.a: Aditi felt annoyed and interrupted, as if someone had grabbed the book away.

qa.q: How could Mummy handle this next time?
qa.a: Mummy could let Aditi finish the chapter first, or ask whether Aditi wants company, instead of forcing Aditi to join in.

qa.q: How does Kiran see Aditi's reading alone?
qa.a: Kiran sees it as boring or a sign of sadness, not understanding that Aditi feels content alone.

grounding: A child happily reads alone and feels content, and being pushed to socialise feels like an intrusion.
